open-question.question: The alternatives pass dispatches one subagent per open question, all at once where the host allows parallel dispatch and one after another where it does not, with no cap. Codex runs subagents in parallel but limits how many subagent threads a session may hold open at once. How should the pass behave on a host that allows parallel dispatch only up to a limit?

recommendation.option: Sliding window at a stated cap

open-question.recommendation: It gives the pass a defined outcome on a question set larger than the cap without the runner having to provoke and interpret a refusal, uses every free slot as each return lands the way the pass already judges returns, and confines the change to the Codex tree so the other two dispatch exactly as written today.

alternative.id: Sliding window at a stated cap

open-question.alternative: Only the Codex tree's dispatch step names an explicit limit: keep at most the session's configured subagent thread cap in flight at once, as Codex's agents.max_threads setting or the default value the prose states. As each question's pipeline finishes (embedded and committed, or skipped after its one repair), its agent is closed and the next pending question is dispatched. The Claude Code and Antigravity trees keep the uncapped all-at-once wording unchanged. Repair by continuation is unaffected, because closing waits for the repair window to end. The runner is told the limit up front, so it never has to provoke and interpret a refusal. The other two host trees can stay byte-identical, because the difference is confined to the Codex tree. It needs a way to deliver Codex-only wording into a core/ step. That mechanism belongs to the Host-specific wording mechanism question, and the build today offers only plugin-root replacement, regex deletion, and frontmatter stripping. The stated number can also drift from the user's actual configuration (the setting is user-editable, and Codex refuses agents.max_threads when multi_agent_v2 is enabled). A stated value that is too high brings back the refusal it was meant to avoid, and one that is too low wastes parallelism.

The pass keeps its current wording: every surviving question is dispatched at once where the host can run several dispatches together, with no cap. Neither core/ nor the Codex host definition adds any wording about a thread limit, so on Codex the host's own limit decides what happens to dispatches beyond it. Spawns past the limit get Codex's "agent thread limit reached" refusal, the prose defines no handling for that refusal, and the runner deals with it however it chooses. No thread is closed explicitly. Nothing in core/, the build, or either existing host tree changes. This milestone's live verification dispatches the alternatives agent only once, so it never comes near the limit and the pass works as written for that run. The pass has no defined outcome when a spawn is refused. This milestone alone holds sixteen open questions, well above a typical cap such as the agents.max_threads value Codex reads from config.toml. A refused spawn may be misread as a failure and skipped, may be retried blindly, or may stall the run. If finished subagent threads keep counting against the cap until they are closed (the Codex binary has a close_agent operation), even the sequential arm would hit the cap partway through. That behaviour is unverified, and when to probe it is up to the Unverified behaviour probes question.

The dispatch step in core/ gets host-neutral wording: dispatch together as many questions as the host will accept. A dispatch the host refuses because its agent limit is reached is not a failure and not a skip. It stays pending and is dispatched again as soon as a running question's pipeline has finished (embedded and committed, or skipped after its one repair). Where the host keeps finished agents open, that question's agent is closed at that point, so the window slides one slot at a time. The prose states no number: the window's size is whatever the host accepts. On a host with no limit the refusal never happens and the wording reduces to today's all-at-once arm. Repair by continuing the same session keeps working, because an agent is closed only once its repair window is over. Codex parallelism is used fully up to whatever limit the user's own configuration sets. The prose needs no stated number and no Codex-only sentence, and it reads correctly on every host, so the Claude Code and Antigravity runs dispatch exactly as they do now. The dispatch sentence in core/ changes, so the Claude Code and Antigravity trees change in text though not in behaviour. Whether that is acceptable depends on the Existing-host preservation bar question. The approach also depends on the runner recognising the limit refusal as distinct from an agent failure, and on Codex releasing a slot when an agent is closed. Neither is yet confirmed by a live run (see the Unverified behaviour probes question).

The dispatch step in core/ gets host-neutral wording: dispatch questions until the host refuses one because its agent limit is reached, or until none are left. The accepted dispatches form a wave. Each return in the wave is judged, repaired once if needed, and committed or skipped as it lands. When the whole wave is done, every agent in it is closed (where the host keeps finished agents open) and the next wave starts from the remaining questions. The prose states no number, and on a host with no limit the first wave holds every question, which is today's behaviour. The bookkeeping is simpler than a sliding window. The runner tracks one batch at a time and closes agents in one sweep at the end of each wave, while the prose still needs no number and no Codex-only sentence. Within each wave the slowest agent holds up the start of the next wave, so slots sit idle and the wall-clock time falls between a sliding window's and the sequential arm's. Like the sliding window, the wording changes the core/ text of every host tree, which depends on the Existing-host preservation bar question. It also relies on the runner recognising the limit refusal and on closing an agent actually freeing a slot, both unconfirmed by a live run.

Only the Codex tree's dispatch step names an explicit wave size: dispatch up to the session's configured subagent thread cap (agents.max_threads, or the default value the prose states). Each return is judged, repaired, and committed or skipped as it lands. When the wave is done, its agents are closed and the next wave of up to the cap begins. The Claude Code and Antigravity trees keep the uncapped all-at-once wording unchanged. It is the most predictable capped behaviour. The runner knows each wave's size before dispatching, never needs to interpret a refusal, and closes agents in one place. The other two host trees can stay byte-identical. It combines the costs of both of its positions. Slots sit idle while the slowest agent of each wave finishes. It needs the Codex-only wording mechanism that the Host-specific wording mechanism question owns. And the stated size can drift from the user's configured cap or from what multi_agent_v2 enforces.

alternative.id: Capped hosts take the sequential arm

open-question.alternative: The existing sequential arm's condition widens, in host-neutral wording in core/, from "where the host cannot run several dispatches at once" to "where it cannot run several at once, or can run only a limited number". On such a host each question is dispatched, judged, repaired at most once, and committed or skipped before the next is dispatched. Its agent is closed once its question is done, where the host keeps finished agents open. No number is stated and no window or wave is tracked. It reuses an arm the pass already defines, which writes the same blocks and lands the same commits. It adds no new dispatch mechanism and needs no Codex-only sentence. At most one subagent thread is ever open, so the cap cannot be reached whatever the user's configuration, and the one open handle keeps repair by continuation trivial. Total token use is the same as a parallel run. It gives up Codex's parallelism entirely, so a large question set takes as long as the slowest serial run. The arm's condition sentence also changes the core/ text of the Claude Code and Antigravity trees, which depends on the Existing-host preservation bar question. And it still relies on closing a finished agent freeing its thread, which is unconfirmed on Codex.

This rejects the premise that the pass should adapt. The dispatch step stays uncapped and unchanged in core/ and in every host tree. Instead, cairn's Codex-facing instructions tell users to raise Codex's subagent thread limit (agents.max_threads in config.toml) high enough to cover the open questions a milestone can hold before they run the alternatives pass. The pass itself never closes threads and never handles a limit refusal. No runtime file changes on any host, so the existing trees are untouched. On a correctly configured Codex session the pass runs in the same all-at-once arm it uses on Claude Code, with full parallelism. Correctness rests on a user setting that cairn cannot check. A question count above the configured value brings back the undefined refusal, and the count a milestone can reach has no upper bound. The setting cannot be used at all once multi_agent_v2 is enabled (Codex rejects agents.max_threads alongside it), and the instruction adds another configuration step to the Codex installation path.
